_link.title: I can explain how crossed electric and magnetic fields act as a velocity selector and derive the selected velocity v = E/B

toLevel2.stem: What is the formula for the selected velocity in a velocity selector?
distractors: v = B/E
v = EB
v = E + B

toLevel2.stem: In a velocity selector, the electric and magnetic fields are oriented so that they are:
distractors: Parallel to each other
At 45° to each other
Antiparallel to each other

toLevel2.stem: What happens to a particle that travels straight through a velocity selector?
toLevel2.answer: The electric and magnetic forces on it are equal and opposite
distractors: It has no charge so neither field affects it
The electric force is much larger than magnetic
The magnetic force is much larger than electric

toLevel2.stem: Which equation shows the condition for a particle to pass through a velocity selector undeflected?
distractors: qE = mv²/r
qV = ½mv²
F = BIl

toLevel2.stem: A velocity selector has E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.060 T. What is the selected velocity?
In a velocity selector, the {{blank:1}} force and the {{blank:2}} force act in opposite directions on the charged particle.
Only particles with speed v = {{blank:1}}/{{blank:2}} travel in a straight line through the selector.
The velocity selector works by balancing the forces qE and {{blank:1}}, which cancels when the speed equals {{blank:2}}.
The selected velocity in a velocity selector depends on the charge of the particle.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A velocity selector uses crossed electric and magnetic fields to allow only particles of a specific speed to pass through.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Why does the selected velocity v = E/B not depend on the charge or mass of the particle?
toLevel3.answer: Both the electric and magnetic forces are proportional to q, so q cancels when the forces are equated
distractors: The charge and mass are too small to affect the balance between the two opposing forces
The electric field only acts on mass while the magnetic field only acts on the charge
The velocity selector is designed to work only for particles of a specific charge value

toLevel3.stem: What happens to a particle moving faster than v = E/B through a velocity selector?
toLevel3.answer: The magnetic force exceeds the electric force and the particle is deflected
distractors: The particle passes straight through because faster particles are unaffected
The electric force exceeds the magnetic force and deflects the particle
The particle slows down to the selected speed and then passes through

toLevel3.stem: What happens to a particle moving slower than v = E/B through a velocity selector?
toLevel3.answer: The electric force exceeds the magnetic force and the particle is deflected
distractors: The particle passes straight through because slow particles are unaffected
The magnetic force exceeds the electric force and deflects the particle
The particle speeds up to the selected velocity and then passes through

toLevel3.stem: Why is a velocity selector important in a mass spectrometer?
toLevel3.answer: It ensures all particles entering the deflection region have the same speed, so differences in radius are due to mass alone
distractors: It separates particles by mass before they enter the magnetic deflection region
It increases the speed of all particles to a value needed for the detector to work
It measures the velocity of each particle so the mass can be calculated directly

toLevel3.stem: In J.J. Thomson's experiment, the electric and magnetic fields were adjusted until the electron beam was undeflected. What did this allow Thomson to calculate?
toLevel3.answer: The speed of the electrons using v = E/B
distractors: The mass of the electrons directly from the balance condition of the two forces
The charge of the electrons from the electric field strength and beam current
The number of electrons in the beam from the total current flowing through it

toLevel3.stem: A velocity selector with E = 1.0 × 10⁵ V/m needs to select particles at 2.5 × 10⁶ m/s. What magnetic field strength is required?
Particles faster than v = E/B are deflected by the {{blank:1}} force, while particles slower than v = E/B are deflected by the {{blank:2}} force.
The charge q cancels in the derivation because both forces are {{blank:1}} to q, making the selected velocity independent of {{blank:2}}.
Thomson used a velocity selector to find v = E/B, and then used a {{blank:1}} field alone to find the {{blank:2}} ratio of the electron.
A velocity selector can select particles of a specific speed regardless of their charge or mass.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: A velocity selector uses E = 4.0 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.20 T. Calculate the selected velocity, and determine whether a proton at 3.0 × 10⁵ m/s would be deflected upward or downward if the electric force is upward.
toLevel4.answer: v = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s; the proton is too fast so the magnetic force dominates and it is deflected downward
distractors: v = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s; the proton is too fast so the electric force dominates and deflects upward
v = 8.0 × 10⁶ m/s; the proton is too slow so the electric force dominates and deflects upward
v = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s; the proton passes straight through because protons are not charge-selected

toLevel4.stem: An engineer needs to select particles at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s. The maximum available magnetic field is 0.50 T. What electric field strength is needed?
A beam contains protons and alpha particles, all at the same speed. Do both pass through the velocity selector?
toLevel4.answer: Yes, because the selected velocity is independent of charge and mass
distractors: No, only protons pass because alpha particles have a different charge
No, only alpha particles pass because they have a greater mass value
Yes, but they exit at different speeds due to their different masses

toLevel4.stem: The electric field in a velocity selector is doubled while B remains constant. What is the new selected velocity?
distractors: The selected velocity halves
The selected velocity stays the same
The selected velocity quadruples

toLevel4.stem: A velocity selector is followed by a magnetic-only deflection region. An ion passes through the selector at speed v = E/B and then curves with radius r in the deflection field B₂. Express the ion's mass in terms of the given quantities.
distractors: m = qEr/B₂ = qErB/B₂
m = qv/B₂r = qE/(B₂rB)
m = qB₂E/rv = qB₂EB/r

toLevel4.stem: In a velocity selector, the plate separation is 0.020 m and the voltage across the plates is 800 V, with B = 0.10 T. What is the selected speed?
A student sets up a velocity selector but accidentally makes the electric and magnetic forces act in the same direction. What happens to the beam?
toLevel4.answer: All particles are deflected in the same direction regardless of speed; no velocity selection occurs
distractors: The selector works normally because only the magnitudes of the forces determine selection
Only particles at twice the normal selected speed pass straight through the selector
The forces cancel for all speeds because they are always equal in a velocity selector

toLevel4.stem: The electric field between parallel plates is E = V/d, so the selected velocity becomes v = {{blank:1}} / ({{blank:2}}).
Doubling the electric field while keeping B constant {{blank:1}} the selected velocity, allowing {{blank:2}} particles to pass.
After passing through the velocity selector, particles enter a deflection region where only the {{blank:1}} field acts, separating them by {{blank:2}}.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether a velocity selector can distinguish between an electron and a proton moving at the same speed.
toLevel5.answer: No; both pass through because v = E/B is independent of charge sign and mass, so the selector cannot distinguish them
distractors: Yes; the electron is deflected differently because it has a negative charge and smaller mass
Yes; the proton passes through while the electron is deflected because of its smaller mass
No; but only because both particles always travel at exactly the same speed in all situations

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that a velocity selector is unnecessary if all particles are accelerated from rest through the same voltage, since they would all have the same kinetic energy. Critique this argument.
toLevel5.answer: Same kinetic energy does not mean same speed; heavier particles are slower, so a velocity selector is still needed for speed uniformity
distractors: The argument is correct; same voltage gives same speed regardless of mass, making a selector redundant
The argument is correct; kinetic energy is what matters for mass spectrometry, not the speed value
The argument is wrong because particles from the same voltage have completely different energies

toLevel5.stem: Compare the roles of the velocity selector and the magnetic deflection region in a mass spectrometer. Why are both stages necessary?
toLevel5.answer: The velocity selector ensures uniform speed; the deflection region then separates by mass. Without uniform speed, radius differences would conflate mass and speed effects.
distractors: The velocity selector separates by mass while the deflection region measures the speed value
Both stages separate by mass independently providing two measurements for greater accuracy
The velocity selector is optional; the deflection region alone can determine both mass and speed

toLevel5.stem: Analyse what would happen if the electric field in a velocity selector were replaced with a gravitational field.
toLevel5.answer: The balance condition would become mg = qvB, making the selected velocity depend on mass and charge, limiting its usefulness
distractors: The selector would work identically because gravity produces the same force as an electric field
The selector would be more effective because gravity acts on all particles regardless of charge
The selector would fail completely because gravity cannot exert any force on charged particles

toLevel5.stem: In Thomson's experiment, after finding v = E/B, he used the magnetic deflection to find q/m. Explain why knowing v was essential for this determination.
toLevel5.answer: The deflection radius depends on both v and q/m, so knowing v allows q/m to be isolated from the radius measurement
distractors: Knowing v was not actually essential; Thomson could have found q/m from the deflection alone
Knowing v allowed Thomson to calculate the total charge on each electron in the beam exactly
Knowing v was needed only to verify his results, not as an essential step in the calculation

toLevel5.stem: Modern velocity selectors use alternating fields (Wien filters with AC). Analyse the advantage of this over static crossed fields.
toLevel5.answer: AC Wien filters can be tuned to select different velocities electronically without physically changing the field strengths
distractors: AC fields select a wider range of speeds simultaneously which is useful for broad beam analysis
AC fields are cheaper to produce than static fields so they reduce the cost of mass spectrometers
AC Wien filters work identically to static ones; there is no practical advantage to using them

toLevel5.stem: Predict how the performance of a velocity selector changes if it is placed in a vacuum versus in air.
toLevel5.answer: In a vacuum the selector works ideally; in air, collisions would scatter particles and reduce the precision of velocity selection
distractors: Air improves performance because the drag ensures all particles reach the same speed quickly
There is no difference because the electric and magnetic forces are unaffected by the medium
In a vacuum the selector fails because the electric field cannot exist without air molecules

toLevel5.stem: A velocity selector passes particles at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s. A particle with 1% higher speed enters. Estimate whether it would be significantly deflected over a 0.10 m selector length.
toLevel5.answer: The force imbalance is small (1% of the total force), producing slight deflection that may or may not be significant depending on slit width
distractors: The particle would be massively deflected because even 1% speed difference creates enormous force imbalance
The particle would not be deflected at all because 1% is within the tolerance of all selectors
The particle would be deflected exactly 1% of the selector length, travelling 1 mm off centre

toLevel5.stem: Thomson used the velocity selector to find v, then used the {{blank:1}} alone to determine the {{blank:2}} ratio of the electron.
The velocity selector is charge-independent because the charge q appears in {{blank:1}} forces and cancels, leaving the selected velocity as a ratio of {{blank:2}} quantities only.
